newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thumbnail sketches of potential Hong Kong leaders.
newsitem.headline: Thumbnail sketches of potential Hong Kong leaders.

text.p: A committee choosing Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader has narrowed the field to three candidates after a first round of voting on Friday.
The 400-member Selection Committee, set up under China's supervision, will cast its final votes on December 11.

Here are sketches of the three candidates, who all have family roots in the mainland city of Shanghai, vying to succeed colonial Governor Chris Patten when Britain hands the colony back to China at midnight next June 30.

TUNG CHEE-HWA - A Shanghai-born shipping tycoon, Tung, 59, is a former member of the governor's advisory Executive Council. He quit as head of Orient Overseas (International) Ltd shipping group to enter the contest and is a vice-chairman of China's Preparatory Committee (PC) on the 1997 handover.

He has strong contacts with China, Taiwan, Britain and the United States. Often tipped as Beijing's favourite for the job as Hong Kong's first chief executive, Tung received 206 of the 400 votes in the first round on November 15.
He is widely respected for his modesty, wisdom, caution, integrity and administrative talent and has been untouched by scandal.

Critics speculate, however, whether he is too beholden to Beijing, who bailed out his family business empire when it was sinking 11 years ago. He is conservative, stresses traditional Chinese values and calls for "consensus and not confrontation" in dealing with China.

YANG TI LIANG - China-born Yang, 67, resigned as Hong Kong's chief justice to run for the top job. He was knighted in 1988, when he became the first Chinese to head the Hong Kong judiciary under British rule. But he dropped the title "Sir" from his name when he entered the leadership contest, opting to be called plain mister. Yang's family moved to Hong Kong from Shanghai after the 1949 communist takeover. He is unpopular with the pro-democracy camp for remarks last year in which he attacked a Bill of Rights introduced by Patten against China's will. In the first-round ballot he came second with 82 votes. Critics say he is weak in administrative talent and indecisive and that he would be putty in Beijing's hands. He has said he would run a "moderately conservative" government if he won.

PETER WOO KWONG-CHING - Shanghai-born tycoon Woo, 50, is a son-in-law of late Hong Kong shipping magnate Sir Yue-kong Pao. The youngest candidate, he is a PC member and honorary chairman of Wharf (Holdings) Ltd and Wheelock and Co Ltd, but he no longer engages in day-to-day running of his companies. He is chairman of Hong Kong's Hospital Authority.

Woo was the first among the candidates to declare a policy platform. He said he would govern Hong Kong and protect its fiscal policies and financial system after the flag change. He came third in the first-round ballot with 54 votes. His detractors say he is too young for the job and less dependable than his elder rivals.
